Of these, all 147 patients with PA-FRI met the inclusion criteria, had completed the final follow-up, and were included in the final analysis. The median follow-up period was 36 months (IQR 30 to 48). The mean age of the cohort was 45.06 years (SD 13.83). Age stratification revealed that the highest incidence of PA-FRI occurred in the 40 to 59 years age group (61.2%; n = 90) followed by the 18 to 39 years age group (24.5%; n = 36). The majority of patients were male (82.3%; n = 121). A total of 90 patients (61.2%; n = 90) had open fractures, and initial osteosynthesis was performed using a plate in 64 patients (43.5%), and a nail in 38 patients (25.9%). The majority of patients (91.8%; n = 135) were classified as Cierny-Mader host type B, indicating a compromised host status. Clinical features such as sinus tract formation were observed in 45.6% (n = 67) of patients. The infection duration was more than ten weeks in 37.4% (n = 55) of cases. Patient demographic and clinical characteristics are summarized in .
Definition and data collection
Clinical outcomes, including infection control, reoperations, and related complications, were followed up in the cohort of patients with PA-FRI. Infection control was evaluated by categorizing cases as either infection persistence or recurrence. Infection persistence was defined as an inadequate response to index debridement and antibiotic therapy, , evidenced by residual signs of infection and imaging or pathological confirmation, or the need for repeat debridement. Infection recurrence was following FRI diagnostic criteria and defined as re-emergent infection at the original site following documented resolution after treatment. , For this, documented infection resolution requires all of the following: no local inflammation (swelling, erythema, warmth, sinus discharge); normal ESR and CRP; no radiological infection signs (e.g. no progressive osteolysis or sequestrum); and negative deep-tissue cultures if clinically indicated. MDR was defined as acquired non-susceptibility to at least one agent in three or more antimicrobial categories. Continuous follow-up was performed at two, six, 12, 18, and 24 months post-treatment. A dedicated clinical researcher (S.W) conducted structured follow-up through scheduled outpatient visits and telephone interviews. Secondary outcomes included reoperation rates, complication profiles, and antimicrobial resistance patterns.
Demographic and clinical variables (e.g. sex, age, infection characteristics, comorbidities, trauma history, tobacco use) as well as treatment parameters (e.g. prior debridements, antibiotic regimens, debridement timing, fixation strategies, flap coverage, and bone reconstruction techniques) were extracted from electronic health records. Microbiological data were obtained from institutional databases, with PA identification based on characteristic colony morphology on blood agar and antimicrobial susceptibility testing via broth microdilution according to the Clinical and Laboratory Standards Institute (CLSI) guidelines. Although CLSI criteria for in vitro susceptibility changed in 2023, we confirm that we consistently used previous CLSI standards for each isolate’s analysis throughout the study period. Based on the consistency of data standards, the 2023 CLSI breakpoint revisions do not affect our results or conclusions.
Statistical analysis
Data were analyzed using SPSS v. 22.0 statistical software (IBM, USA). Intergroup differences in demographic factors, clinical characteristics, treatment protocols, infection cure rates, and postoperative complications were statistically assessed using chi-squared tests for categorical variables and independent-samples t -tests for continuous variables, with normality confirmed via Shapiro-Wilk testing. To elucidate the role of demographic, microbiological, antibiotic, and surgical treatment-related variables as potential risk factors for recurrence, we compared patients with apparent cure to those experiencing recurrence. Fisher’s exact test was used to compare proportions. Variables exhibiting p-values < 0.25 in univariate screening were included in multivariable logistic regression analysis to evaluate their independent associations after adjustment for confounders. Where applicable, 95% CIs and p-values were calculated to determine statistical significance. Statistical significance was defined as a two-sided p-value < 0.05.

Results
Microbiological profile and antimicrobial resistance
In terms of microbial aetiology, PA was the sole pathogen in 72 (49.0%) of cases, while coinfection with S. aureus occurred in 17 (11.5%) of cases. Coinfection with other pathogens accounted for 58 (39.5%) of cases. Notably, the prevalence of PA among all Gram-negative bacilli FRI isolates was 34.6% (n = 147 out of 425), which was slightly increased from 28.4% (n = 29 out of 102) in 2012 to 2014 to 39.3% (n= 33 out of 84) in 2021 to 2023 ( ). Among these, the total prevalence of MDR-PA was as high as 44.9% (n = 66 out of 147) in this study period, significantly increased from 33.3% (n = 11 out of 33) in 2012 to 2014 to 48.0% (n = 24 out of 50) in 2018 to 2020, and to 58.6%(n = 17 out of 29) in 2021 to 2023 ( ). For specific antimicrobial agents, piperacillin, cefazolin, cefuroxime, Chemitrim, and minocycline resistance levels in PA were nearly 100% (n = 147 ). The proportion of PA infections resistant to carbapenems (e.g. imipenem, meropenem) was also of concern, reaching as high as 31%(n = 45 out of 147). Details of the microbiological profiles and antimicrobial resistance are shown in and .

Treatment methods and clinical outcomes
Initial debridement and antibiotic therapy were the mainstay of treatment. The median duration of intravenous antibiotic therapy was four weeks (IQR 3 to 5 weeks). Some patients also received oral antibiotics, which were administered following the completion of intravenous therapy as sequential therapy. The median duration of oral antibiotic therapy was two weeks (IQR 1 to 3 weeks). All antibiotic therapy is individualized by a multidisciplinary team based on culture and susceptibility results, as well as the patient’s clinical response. Duration was calculated from the first day of effective intravenous antibiotics to the cessation of all systemic antibiotics (intravenous or oral). Additionally, 80.3% (n = 118) of patients were treated with local antibiotics via antibiotic-loaded polymethylmethacrylate (PMMA) ( and ). Ceftazidime and piperacillin/tazobactam were the most commonly used intravenous antibiotics, while 5 g of vancomycin was added to 40 g PMMA (containing 0.5 g gentamicin) for local treatment. Initial infection control was achieved in 132 patients (89.8%), with 10.2% (n = 15) experiencing infection persistence after the first treatment, and 48 patients (32.7%) needed additional flap coverage. Following initial infection control, 123 patients (83.7%) underwent reconstruction surgery for larger bone defects. Autografts were used in 64 patients, bone transport in 37 patients, and permanent PMMA retention in 22 patients. However, 23 patients (15.6%) experienced recurrence ( and ), 13 (56.5%) within six months, seven (30.4%) between six and 12 months, and three (13.1%) beyond 12 months, after documented resolution of infection. Among the 23 patients with recurrence, 11 had a positive culture for PA again, while 12 were culture-negative. At the end of the follow-up, nine patients (6.1%) required amputation (seven due to refractory infection and two due to malignancy), while the remaining 14 patients achieved infection-free bone union.

Risk factors of recurrence
Univariate analysis revealed that factors such as age, sex, tobacco use, prior fractures, previous debridement, prior implant use, Cierny–Mader host type, sinus formation, bone reconstruction, and use of local antibiotics were not associated with infection recurrence ( ). Fisher’s exact test showed MDR infection (p = 0.002), use of less than four weeks of systemic antibiotics (p < 0.001), flap coverage (p = 0.014), post-debridement internal fixation (p = 0.009), and long-term PMMA retention (p = 0.008) were potential influencing factors for recurrence. Multivariate logistic regression analysis ( ) revealed that post-debridement internal fixation (OR 4.85 (95% CI 1.00 to 23.36); p = 0.049) and prior multiple debridements (two or more) (OR 6.00 (95% CI 1.02 to 35.37); p = 0.048) were associated with an increased risk of recurrence in PA-FRI. Additionally, MDR-PA infection (OR 11.33 (95% CI 1.95 to 65.91); p = 0.007), long-term PMMA spacer retention (OR 9.32 (95% CI 2.08 to 41.80); p = 0.004), and use of less than four weeks of systemic antibiotics (OR 7.84 (95% CI 2.02 to 30.40); p = 0.003) were identified as strong predictors of recurrence. Conversely, surgical intervention in the late infection phase (more than ten weeks) (OR 0.16 (95% CI 0.04 to 0.63); p = 0.009) was associated with a reduced risk of recurrence compared with interventions in the acute or sub-acute phase.

Forest plot showing odds ratios and confidence intervals for factors associated with outcomes in bone infection treatment. The image is a forest plot summarizing odds ratios (ORs), 95% confidence intervals (CIs), and p values for ten clinical variables associated with a treatment outcome. A vertical reference line at OR = 1 indicates no effect, and each variable is represented by a black dot with horizontal confidence interval bars. Variables with statistically significant associations (p < 0.05) include systemic antibiotics for less than 4 weeks versus longer treatment (OR 7.84, 95% CI 2.02–30.40, p = 0.003), permanent PMMA retention versus no retention (OR 9.32, 95% CI 2.08–41.80, p = 0.004), multidrug-resistant infection versus non-resistant infection (OR 11.33, 95% CI 1.95–65.91, p = 0.007), infection duration greater than 10 weeks versus shorter duration (OR 0.16, 95% CI 0.04–0.63, p = 0.009), prior multiple debridements of two or more versus one or none (OR 6.00, 95% CI 1.02–35.37, p = 0.048), and post-debridement internal fixation versus none (OR 4.85, 95% CI 1.00–23.36, p = 0.049). fullTextSections.discussion:
Discussion
PA-FRI presents a formidable clinical challenge due to the pathogen’s intrinsic biofilm-forming capacity, adaptive antibiotic resistance, and ability to colonize medical devices. Our 12-year retrospective cohort study analyzing 147 PA-FRI cases underscored the persistent threat posed by antibiotic resistance and the high recurrence rates associated with this infection. Results demonstrated that 44.9% (n = 66) of isolates were identified as MDR, including carbapenem-resistant PA, with a recurrence rate of 15.6% (n = 23) despite aggressive debridement and antimicrobial treatment. These findings were consistent with global trends and present huge therapeutic challenges due to limited treatment options and increased morbidity. ,
In our cohort, tibial fractures were most prevalent (69.4%; n = 102), likely due to compromised soft-tissue coverage and delayed vascularization, which provide a conducive environment for adhesion of biofilm bacteria (e.g. PA). , Most patients had undergone multiple surgeries and repeated antimicrobial treatments, which inevitably aggravates the development of drug resistance. Those patients with multiple revision surgeries (two or more) faced a six-fold higher risk of recurrence, underscoring the complex nature of these cases. The recurrence may stem from hidden infection niches and compromised local immunity due to repeated surgeries, consistent with previous reports. , , Coinfections were also common in our study. In particular, these coinfections may enhance the resilience of PA biofilms via extracellular matrix cross-talk. , - However, no significant correlation was found between coinfections and recurrence in subsequent analyses. MDR-PA was found to be a strong predictor of recurrence, highlighting the critical need for effective antimicrobial stewardship and the development of novel therapeutic strategies to address MDR-PA infections.
The combination of appropriate surgical intervention with antimicrobial therapy remains the standard approach in orthopaedic infection management. Current evidence suggests that both oral and intravenous antibiotics are effective in treating these infections. , - The general recommendation is for systemic antibiotics to be administered for at least four to six weeks post-surgery, but the duration of treatment often depends on clinician experience, therapy response, and patient-specific factors such as compliance and tolerability. Prolonged antibiotic therapy, however, increases the risk of hepatorenal toxicity, gut dysbiosis, secondary infections, and accelerated development of resistant strains. , , , Some authors have previously suggested that shorter courses of systemic antibiotics, especially when combined with local antibiotic therapy, can achieve good outcomes. - In our study, the use of systemic antibiotics for less than four weeks was identified as a significant risk factor for recurrence, emphasizing the importance of adequate and appropriate antibiotic therapy in the management of PA-FRI.
To date, there is no universally accepted classification of FRI. Some scholars have attempted to classify infection duration in relation to fractures into early infection (within two weeks), delayed infection (three to ten weeks), and late infection (more than ten weeks). , , In our study, we observed that debridement performed during the late infection phase significantly reduced the risk of recurrence compared with interventions in the early or delayed phases (p = 0.009). This may be explained by the fact that, during the late phase, the infection is often more localized, allowing for better delineation of necrotic tissue, which can be more thoroughly excised. , , Clinically, this may support a staged approach to treatment: initial antibiotic therapy or drainage, followed by definitive debridement during the chronic phase. However, this finding must be interpreted cautiously: optimal timing remains a case-by-case decision, depending on patient stability and soft-tissue condition.
In the management of FRI, stabilization and reconstruction following debridement are often considered necessary steps for most patients. While external fixation has long been the standard method for treating orthopaedic infections, there is an increasing trend towards using antibiotic-loaded bone cement in combination with internal fixation, , , primarily as a temporary solution. The theoretical basis for this approach lies in the coating strategies that enhance local antimicrobial therapy and reduce bacterial adhesion. Bone grafting, the induced membrane technique, and bone transport remain the primary methods for managing large bone defects. However, with the widespread use of antibiotic-loaded bone cement (PMMA), some patients may opt for permanent PMMA spacers for bone defects. In our study, both post-debridement internal fixation and long-term PMMA spacer retention were identified as significant risk factors for recurrence in PA-FRI. These findings suggest that the use of internal fixation and long-term retention of PMMA spacers should be approached with caution.
There are several limitations in this study. First, selection bias may have been introduced by the single-centre nature of the study. Second, not all confounders that could influence antibiotic response, such as socioeconomic factors and first line antibiotic choice, were included in the analysis. Third, the relatively small number of recurrence events (n = 23) limited statistical power for multivariable analysis, and some statistically significant differences have wide CIs. Despite these limitations, this study remains the largest cohort of PA-FRI cases with extended follow-up, providing valuable insights into recurrence patterns and management.
This 12-year analysis of 147 PA-FRI cases highlighted the growing prevalence of MDR and substantial recurrence risks, underscoring the therapeutic complexity inherent in PA-FRI. Several non-modifiable and modifiable risk factors were identified as being associated with infection recurrence, contributing to management for preoperative optimization, antimicrobial stewardship, and surgical decision-making.

Take home message

- This study identified that systemic antibiotics < four weeks, post-debridement internal fixation, and retained polymethylmethacrylate spacers are modifiable risk factors for recurrence of Pseudomonas aeruginosa (PA) fracture-related infection.
- High multidrug-resistant PA prevalence (44.9%) independently predicted recurrence, highlighting the need for enhanced antimicrobial stewardship and tailored surgical decision-making.
